templates.title: Weekend camping
templates.blurb: A short trip to a campground or national park.
templates.region: Australia-wide; park rules are from NSW National Parks, so check your state

items.text: Tell a trusted person your route, who is with you, and when you expect to be back. Agree a time to check in.

guides.title: Tell someone your plans

items.text: Check whether you need to book, and that camping is allowed where you are going.

items.text: Check park alerts and closures and the weather forecast. In NSW, use the Hazards Near Me app.

guides.title: Camping in national parks: booking, water and first aid

items.text: Check the fire danger rating and the fire rules for your state. No fires in the open on a Total Fire Ban day.

guides.title: Bushfire: before you travel
Total Fire Bans: what is allowed

items.text: Download the Emergency+ app before you leave. It only works with mobile reception.

guides.title: Emergency+ app and giving your location

items.text: Check your camping equipment works before you leave.

guides.title: Camping in national parks: booking, water and first aid

items.text: Carry enough drinking water. Most campgrounds do not have any. See the water guide for each agency's figures.

items.text: Food for every day of the trip, plus extra in case of delays.

items.text: Hat, sunscreen and insect repellent. Put repellent on after sunscreen.

items.text: Tarpaulin or other shade, and a blanket.

guides.title: What to pack for remote driving

items.text: Cooler or fridge, rubbish bags, toilet paper, and matches or a lighter.

items.text: Bring your own firewood if fires are allowed. Do not collect fallen timber.

items.text: Look up when you set up. Check for loose, dead or overhanging tree limbs.

items.text: Camp above flood and tide debris. Do not camp in dry creek beds or road drains.

guides.title: Choosing and setting up a campsite

items.text: Always supervise children near rivers, lakes and creeks.

guides.title: Choosing and setting up a campsite

items.text: Keep a fire attended with water ready, at least 2 metres from anything that can burn. Put it out completely before bed or before you leave.

guides.title: Campfire safety

templates.title: Remote 4WD trip
templates.blurb: Unsealed roads and tracks, a long way from help.
templates.region: Australia-wide; much of the advice is from Queensland Parks, NSW National Parks and South Australia

items.text: Tell someone where you are going and when you expect to return. Tell them when you arrive.

guides.title: Tell someone your plans
4WD before you go

items.text: Calculate distances, check refuelling points and allow plenty of time. Do not make the schedule too tight.

guides.title: 4WD before you go
Plan your route and check conditions

items.text: Check which roads and tracks you are allowed to drive, and whether any are closed.

guides.title: 4WD before you go
Plan your route and check conditions

items.text: Check the weather forecast, park alerts and closures, and road conditions before you go. Unsealed roads may be impassable after rain.

guides.title: Plan your route and check conditions

items.text: Pack detailed paper maps. GPS and other navigation devices may stop working in some conditions.

guides.title: 4WD before you go
Plan your route and check conditions

items.text: Be proficient in 4WD driving. If you are a novice, drive with an experienced four-wheel driver.

guides.title: 4WD before you go

items.text: Have the vehicle serviced before a remote journey.

guides.title: Vehicle checks before a long trip

items.text: Tyres in good condition and at the right pressure, including the spares. Check the maker's pressure advice for the terrain.

guides.title: Vehicle checks before a long trip
4WD before you go

items.text: Check brake, coolant, oil, clutch, automatic transmission, power steering and water levels.

guides.title: Vehicle checks before a long trip

items.text: Check the battery, and the fan belt condition and tension. Check coolant hoses for leaks.

guides.title: Vehicle checks before a long trip

items.text: Check headlights, high beams, reverse, indicators, brake lights and windscreen wipers.

guides.title: Vehicle checks before a long trip

items.text: Consider roadside assistance through your state motoring organisation.

guides.title: Vehicle checks before a long trip

items.text: Two spare tyres, both inflated, and a strong jack.

guides.title: Spares, tools and recovery gear
What to pack for remote driving

items.text: A long-handled shovel.

guides.title: Spares, tools and recovery gear
What to pack for remote driving

items.text: A tool kit for the vehicle, including tyre-changing equipment. Queensland lists a jack, winder, wheel brace, spanners, screwdrivers, a spare fan belt, hoses and fuses.

guides.title: What to pack for remote driving

items.text: On sand trips, carry a tyre gauge, air pump and traction aids.

guides.title: Spares, tools and recovery gear

items.text: Good recovery gear, and know how to use it before you need it. Tow ropes and snatch straps are for trained operators with safety-rated equipment only.

guides.title: Spares, tools and recovery gear
4WD before you go

items.text: A fire extinguisher.

guides.title: What to pack for remote driving
Spares, tools and recovery gear

items.text: Take reliable communication equipment, such as a satellite phone or a UHF radio.

guides.title: 4WD before you go
Satellite phones and HF radio

items.text: Take a personal locator beacon (PLB). It must be registered with AMSA. Only set it off if you are in danger or injured.

guides.title: Personal locator beacons (PLBs)
4WD before you go

items.text: Download the Emergency+ app. It only works with mobile reception.

guides.title: Emergency+ app and giving your location

items.text: Water: Queensland and NSW say 20 litres for emergency use plus 4 litres per person per day. Other agencies give other figures, so read the water guide.

guides.title: What to pack for remote driving
How much water to carry

items.text: Food for every day, plus extra to cover delays.

guides.title: What to pack for remote driving

items.text: Enough fuel between all stops. For remote trips, consider extra fuel in a suitable container. Soft sand, mud and hills use more.

guides.title: Plan your fuel stops

items.text: First aid kit, including a snake bite kit.

guides.title: What to pack for remote driving

items.text: A summary of your medical history, all your medication and repeat scripts.

guides.title: Medical readiness for remote travel

items.text: Take a break every 2 hours. Do not drive for more than 8 to 10 hours a day.

guides.title: Driver fatigue: breaks and daily limits

items.text: If you break down or are stranded, stay with your vehicle.

templates.title: Caravan pre-departure
templates.blurb: Checks before you hitch up and during the trip.
templates.region: NSW rules and guidance. Other states have their own rules, so check each state you will drive in

items.text: Know your caravan's ATM and GTM and your tow ball weight. Know your vehicle's maximum towing capacity, and its GCM if the maker gives one.

guides.title: Caravan weights: know your numbers

items.text: Weigh the loaded caravan and vehicle at a weigh station. Non-compliance may affect your insurance, and unsafe loading can lead to fines.

guides.title: Caravan weights: know your numbers

items.text: Do not exceed the rated capacity of the towbar and coupling, which should be marked on the towbar.

guides.title: Brakes, safety chains and couplings

items.text: Keep heavy items towards the centre, low and close to the axle.

guides.title: Loading a caravan

items.text: Aim for about 60 per cent of the weight forward of the axle centre.

guides.title: Loading a caravan

items.text: About 5 to 10 per cent of the total mass should rest on the vehicle through the coupling.

guides.title: Loading a caravan

items.text: The drawbar should be level or slightly nose down.

guides.title: Loading a caravan

items.text: Secure and contain the load. Do not overload.

guides.title: Loading a caravan

items.text: Also use the Transport for NSW caravan safety checklist.

guides.title: Loading a caravan

items.text: The coupling is locked and strong enough for a fully loaded trailer.

guides.title: Brakes, safety chains and couplings

items.text: Safety chains are connected to the towing vehicle, as short as practicable, and crossed over if two are fitted.

guides.title: Brakes, safety chains and couplings
Caravan checks before and during a trip

items.text: Over 2 tonnes gross trailer mass: an automatic breakaway system is fitted, and brakes can be operated from the driver's seat.

guides.title: Brakes, safety chains and couplings

items.text: All lights work.

guides.title: Caravan checks before and during a trip

items.text: Wheel bearings, suspension and brakes work properly.

guides.title: Caravan checks before and during a trip

items.text: All tyres, on the vehicle and the caravan, are properly inflated.

guides.title: Caravan checks before and during a trip
Vehicle checks before a long trip

items.text: Vehicle and caravan are roadworthy.

guides.title: Caravan checks before and during a trip

items.text: Oil, water, brake fluid, battery and other vehicle service checks are done.

guides.title: Caravan checks before and during a trip

items.text: Tow bar and connections are in good order.

guides.title: Vehicle checks before a long trip

items.text: Plan to refuel more often. Fuel use rises when towing, especially over 90 km/h.

guides.title: Plan your fuel stops

items.text: Plan fewer hours on the road each day and more rest breaks. Towing is more tiring.

guides.title: Driver fatigue: breaks and daily limits

items.text: At regular stops, check couplings, doors, hatches, covers and the load are still secure.

guides.title: Caravan checks before and during a trip

items.text: At regular stops, check tyres are still inflated and not rubbing on suspension or bodywork.

templates.title: Extreme heat
templates.blurb: Travelling or camping in very hot weather.
templates.region: Australia-wide; NT advice for the Red Centre and Top End

items.text: Plan around the heat. Avoid being outdoors between 11am and 3pm, and avoid physical activity.

guides.title: Staying well in hot weather

items.text: The Royal Flying Doctor Service advises against travelling in the hottest part of the year.

guides.title: Best time to travel: heat, cold and the wet season

items.text: Heat adds to fatigue. Drink water and take regular breaks.

guides.title: Driver fatigue: breaks and daily limits
Driving a vehicle in extreme heat

items.text: Drink plenty of water, even if you are not thirsty.

guides.title: Staying well in hot weather
Dehydration: signs and prevention

items.text: In the Red Centre and Top End, the NT Government says to drink at least 1 litre of water an hour when outside.

guides.title: How much water to carry

items.text: Carry enough water. Needs are higher in extremely hot climates and with hard exertion, so treat the agency figures as a starting point.

guides.title: How much water to carry

items.text: Wear light-coloured, loose-fitting clothes, sunscreen and a hat. Stay out of the sun.

guides.title: Staying well in hot weather
Sun protection

items.text: Slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat, seek shade, slide on sunglasses.

guides.title: Sun protection

items.text: Cool showers or baths help. Use fans or air conditioning if you can.

guides.title: Staying well in hot weather

items.text: Check coolant, engine oil, brake fluid and power steering fluid.

guides.title: Driving a vehicle in extreme heat

items.text: Check tyre pressure before heading off, and check tread depth.

guides.title: Driving a vehicle in extreme heat

items.text: Watch the temperature gauge.

guides.title: Driving a vehicle in extreme heat

items.text: Carry jumper leads, a torch, a phone charger, and extra coolant for long distances.

guides.title: Driving a vehicle in extreme heat

items.text: Older vehicles: carry a litre of oil and check the level regularly.

guides.title: Driving a vehicle in extreme heat

items.text: Never leave babies, children or animals alone in a car, even with the air conditioner on.

guides.title: Never leave children or animals in a hot car

items.text: Animals outside need water and plenty of shade.

guides.title: Never leave children or animals in a hot car

items.text: Check on older friends, neighbours and relatives in hot weather. People at higher risk include those over 65, babies and young children, people with long-term health conditions, and people not used to the heat.

guides.title: Staying well in hot weather
Never leave children or animals in a hot car

items.text: Know the signs of dehydration and heat illness. If someone is confused, collapsing or very unwell in the heat, see the Heatstroke card and call 000.

templates.title: Flood season
templates.blurb: Travelling where heavy rain and flooding are likely.
templates.region: Australia-wide; NSW, Victoria, NT and Queensland agency advice

items.text: Check the weather forecast, warnings and road conditions before you go and again along the way.

guides.title: Plan your route and check conditions
Bushfire: before you travel

items.text: Northern Territory wet season: some roads and tracks can become impassable. Check the NT road report before you leave.

guides.title: Plan your route and check conditions
Best time to travel: heat, cold and the wet season

items.text: Set watch zones for floods and severe weather in the Hazards Near Me app (NSW SES). Apps and alerts need mobile reception.

guides.title: Australian Warning System levels

items.text: Know the warning levels: Advice, Watch and Act, Emergency Warning.

guides.title: Australian Warning System levels

items.text: Note the SES number, 132 500. In a life-threatening emergency, call 000.

guides.title: Getting SES help in floods and storms

items.text: Creeks can rise suddenly and you may be cut off for days after heavy rain. Carry extra food and water.

guides.title: Flooded roads and creek crossings
What to pack for remote driving

items.text: Camp above flood and tide debris. Do not camp in dry creek beds or road drains.

guides.title: Choosing and setting up a campsite

items.text: Check the forecast. In wet weather you may not be able to reach or leave the campground.

guides.title: Choosing and setting up a campsite

items.text: Never drive through floodwater. If it is flooded, forget it.

guides.title: Flooded roads and creek crossings

items.text: It takes just 15 cm of flowing water to float a small car. Floodwater can hide potholes, debris and washed-away road surfaces.

guides.title: Flooded roads and creek crossings

items.text: Turn around on flooded roads and find a safer way. Only travel if it is essential.

guides.title: Flooded roads and creek crossings

items.text: If driving is dangerous, pull over safely on higher ground, away from trees.

guides.title: Flooded roads and creek crossings

items.text: If you are trapped in your car by rising flash floods, call 000. See the Flood card.

guides.title: Flooded roads and creek crossings

items.text: Leave early, before roads are closed. If you stay, it may be too dangerous to rescue you.

guides.title: Getting SES help in floods and storms

items.text: The SES may not be able to reach you straight away. You may need to rely on yourself and others for a while.

guides.title: Getting SES help in floods and storms

items.text: Stay at your safe location. Going to look at affected areas makes the response harder.

guides.title: Getting SES help in floods and storms

items.text: Throw out food and drink, including water, that has touched floodwater.

guides.title: Flooded roads and creek crossings
